stories.title: A Narrow Sea Passage Could Change Prices Everywhere
stories.headline_kid: A tiny stretch of sea near Iran carries oil for the whole world — and a US leader just said he might claim it as American land.
summary: Imagine a single-lane bridge that almost every truck in the world must cross to deliver goods. The Strait of Hormuz is like that, but for oil ships. It is a narrow strip of sea between Iran and its neighbours, and a huge share of the world's oil sails through it every single day.

US President Donald Trump said on Friday that American forces have already stopped ships from passing through unless the US allows it. He also said he plans to soon declare this waterway as United States territory, after what he calls defeating Iran.

This matters because when oil struggles to move freely, its price usually goes up. Singapore does not produce its own oil, so it buys fuel from other countries and is also one of the world's busiest ports for oil trading and shipping.

If oil becomes more expensive, petrol for cars, bus and taxi fares, and even the cost of flying could rise here too. Families might notice this when grocery shopping or filling up the car, since transporting goods becomes costlier.

lenses.me: If oil prices rise, things you buy — like snacks or toys shipped from other countries — might cost a little more.
lenses.family: Your family might notice slightly higher transport costs, like petrol, bus fares or even flight tickets for holidays.
lenses.friends: Your friends' families who drive or travel a lot might feel the pinch of rising fuel prices first.
lenses.nation: Singapore is a major oil-trading and shipping hub, so trouble in the Strait of Hormuz can affect our economy and cost of living.
lenses.world: Since so much of the world's oil passes through this strait, tension there can push up prices and costs for almost every country.

stories.title: Health Minister Finds His Army Buddy After Almost 40 Years
stories.headline_kid: Singapore's Health Minister was reunited with the friend who helped him through tough army training decades ago!
summary: In Singapore, most young men go through National Service (NS), where they train to protect the country. It can be tough, especially during Basic Military Training (BMT), the very first and hardest stage.

Health Minister Ong Ye Kung and a recruit named Eric Sim were paired up during their BMT because they happened to share the same birthday. The two 'chill' friends leaned on each other to get through the hardship together.

After about three months of training together, they lost touch, as often happens when NS ends and life moves on. Nearly 40 years later, they finally met again for a TV programme called On The Red Dot.
Their reunion brought back warm memories of friendship and the tough moments they overcame side by side. It shows how the bonds made during NS can stay meaningful, even after decades apart.

lenses.me: If you have a good friend, remember that even years apart, true friendships can be found again.
lenses.family: Your dad, uncle or grandfather may have similar NS stories — this is a good excuse to ask them!
lenses.friends: It shows how shared hardships, like tough training or exams, can create friendships that last a lifetime.
lenses.nation: NS is something almost every Singaporean man goes through — it's a shared experience that shapes our nation's identity.
lenses.world: Many countries have their own versions of national service, and stories like this show how shared duty can build lasting bonds.

stories.title: Schools in Thailand Tighten Safety Checks After a Sad Shooting
stories.headline_kid: After a shooting hurt people at a school last week, Bangkok schools are now checking bags and watching entrances much more carefully.
summary: Last week, a shooting at a school in Thailand caused great sadness and shock. To keep students safe, the Bangkok city government has now ordered all schools under its care to tighten security.
Schools must now check bags, pockets, and even pencil cases for weapons. Guards will be on duty around the clock, and visitors must follow strict rules before they can enter school grounds.
On Friday, students quietly lined up while teachers checked their belongings before school began — a new routine that shows how seriously the country is taking student safety.

While this happened far from Singapore, it reminds us how important school safety measures are everywhere. Singapore schools already have some safety steps, like visitor passes and security guards, to help keep students safe every day.

lenses.me: It might make you think about the safety rules at your own school, like wearing a visitor pass or having a guard at the gate.
lenses.family: Parents everywhere want their children to feel safe at school — this news might spark conversations at home about safety.
lenses.friends: Your classmates might also feel for the students in Thailand and appreciate the safety measures at your own school.
lenses.nation: Singapore already has strong school safety systems, and stories like this remind us why these rules matter.
lenses.world: Schools around the world are learning from each other on how to keep students safe from danger.

stories.title: Record Rain in Japan Leaves 8 Dead and Thousands Stuck at the Airport
stories.headline_kid: Heavy rain in Japan has flooded towns, cut power to over 20,000 homes, and stranded thousands of travellers — sadly, at least 8 people have died.
summary: Japan has been hit by record-breaking rain this week, especially in the Chiba region near Tokyo. The rain was so heavy that weather forecasters issued their highest-level warning for the area for the very first time.

The flooding caused landslides, cut power to more than 20,000 homes, and left thousands of travellers stranded at Narita Airport, one of Japan's busiest airports. Sadly, at least 8 people have died because of the disaster.

Many families travel to Japan for holidays, especially during the school break, so this news matters for anyone with travel plans there. Flights have been delayed and disrupted because of the extreme weather.

This story reminds us how quickly weather can change and disrupt travel plans. If your family is planning a trip anywhere, it's always wise to check weather updates and flight status before heading to the airport.

lenses.me: If your family is planning a holiday to Japan, this is a reminder to always check the weather forecast beforehand.
lenses.family: Parents planning trips might need to reschedule flights or activities if bad weather strikes.
lenses.friends: Classmates who are travelling during the school holidays might share similar travel disruption stories.
lenses.nation: Singapore Airlines and other airlines flying to Japan may need to adjust schedules because of extreme weather like this.
lenses.world: Extreme weather events like this are becoming more common everywhere, reminding us how climate change can affect daily life.

stories.title: Can the Lions Finally Beat Thailand After 14 Years?
stories.headline_kid: Singapore's football team, the Lions, face Thailand in the ASEAN Championship semi-finals — and they haven't won against them in 14 years!
summary: Singapore's national football team, nicknamed the Lions, will play Thailand in the semi-finals of the ASEAN Championship. It has been about 14 years since Singapore last beat Thailand in a match — a long losing streak!
Head coach Gavin Lee says the team won't let this past record define or 'own' them. He believes the players are ready to fight hard and focus on the present match, not old history.
The match will be played at Jalan Besar Stadium, and fans across Singapore will be cheering the Lions on, hoping to finally break the long streak against their rivals.
This match is a great chance for the team to show growth and determination. Win or lose, it's a reminder that hard work and self-belief matter more than what happened in the past.

lenses.me: If you play sports, this story shows that you shouldn't let past losses stop you from trying your best next time.
lenses.family: Your family might gather to watch the match together and cheer for the Singapore team.
lenses.friends: You and your friends might talk about the match at school and support the Lions together.
lenses.nation: A win against Thailand would be a huge boost for Singapore football and national pride.
lenses.world: The ASEAN Championship brings together countries across Southeast Asia in friendly sporting competition.
